sweep_summary: Momu-Fas (fass1245) is in the catalog as UNDETERMINED on Honeyman 2017 p.461 (compound bears a single prominent accent; no placement rule). The sweep's only keyword item, Brendel & Ackermann 2009 'Foreign Accent Syndrome (FAS)', is a neurology chapter matched on the language name and is irrelevant (Crossref record confirms; paywalled; priority none). Re-read the three SIL Fas phonology documents already on file from the 9/16 audit and the Honeyman thesis text: Baron 2007 (p.6) and Baron 1983c (pp.3, 6) attest stress as a conditioning factor ('unstressed syllables and heavily stressed syllables'; '/ey/ and /ow/ only occur in stressed open syllables'; 'a fuller analysis of stress' still needed), and the SIL OPD's Suprasegmentals section is blank; the OPD's acute accents mark mid vowels, not stress. Honeyman's compound passage re-read verbatim, matches the catalog quote; his phonology chapter has no stress section. No source states where word stress falls, so the coding stays UNDETERMINED with Baron 2007 as supporting evidence that word stress exists. Glottolog's only other sketch, Blake 2007 'Spatial Reference in Momu' (Sydney thesis), has no open copy located (low priority).

new_statements.quote: [ə] in Fas occurs in closed syllables, unstressed syllables and heavily stressed syllables. It may be inserted between incompatible consonant sequences. It has not been noticed to occur word finally. There is some evidence that it represents /i/ in these positions.
new_statements.citation: Baron, Wietze. 2007. Overview of Fas Phonology. Ms, 8 pp. SIL PNG (SIL Language & Culture Archives item 50902).
new_statements.reading: The SIL fieldworker who worked on Fas for decades treats stress as a real, gradient property of Fas syllables (unstressed vs heavily stressed) that conditions schwa, and in his 1983 orthography paper also ties /ey/ /ow/ to 'stressed open syllables' while conceding stress has not been fully analysed. This is independent first-hand confirmation that Momu-Fas has word-level stress, but neither Baron paper nor Honeyman 2017 states where it falls, so the catalog's UNDETERMINED (accent exists per phonological word, position unstated) stands.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Honeyman 2017 PDF at PDF p.490, ex. (14.16); only correction is cosmetic - printed page is 462 (not 461; §14.1.2.2 starts on 461). The negative finding (no stress/accent placement rule anywhere in ch.2 or elsewhere; only accent-marked forms are ke(y)-fukú / úikeno) was re-verified by TOC inspection and full-text grep. (2) Deciding source is a 700-pp 2017 ANU PhD reference grammar by the language's documenter - the best and only full description; Glottolog's other 'grammar/phonology' entries for fass1245 are spurious Chomsky-Halle bibliography matches, plus Baron's SIL segmental papers (held) and a 2007 honours thesis on spatial reference. sources.citation: Baron, Wietze. 2007. Overview of Fas Phonology. Ms, 8 pp. SIL PNG (SIL Language & Culture Archives item 50902).
sources.quote: [ə] in Fas occurs in closed syllables, unstressed syllables and heavily stressed syllables. It may be inserted between incompatible consonant sequences. It has not been noticed to occur word finally. There is some evidence that it represents /i/ in these positions.
sources.note: Attests that Fas has word stress with degrees ('unstressed' vs 'heavily stressed' syllables) conditioning schwa; no statement anywhere in the 8 pp of where stress falls (no stress section; the paper is about the vowel system). Grep of the whole text for stress/accent/tone/pitch/prosod yields only this sentence.

sources.quote: The 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' section is blank. Only indirect mentions: 'A fuller analysis of stress may render schwa non-phonemic.' and 'The phonemic status of schwa is unsure. It only occurs on the unstressed closed syllables, and is left unwritten in this proposal.' No placement rule.

sources.note: SIL OPD sheets carry a dedicated 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' slot; for Fas it is blank, which independently corroborates that no stress-placement analysis exists (record rests on Honeyman's silence).
